title: Which choke for which distance
summary: A rough guide to chokes for close, medium and far targets in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, plus advice for beginners.

body.html: Distance to the target is the main factor in choosing a choke. The two disciplines set their distances in different ways.

html.sporting: Targets imitate hunting shots, so they are set at distances where a hunter could cleanly shoot a bird. They are not so close that the meat would be ruined, and not so far that the bird would only be wounded. The rules call this hunting ethics.
html.compak: Targets fly over a marked rectangle 35–40 m wide and 25 m deep in front of the shooting positions.

html: Up to about 20 m: cylinder or a very light choke (1/8).
About 20–30 m: improved cylinder (1/4) or light modified.
Beyond about 35 m: improved modified (3/4), and occasionally full.

body.html: This is a rough guide that many coaches use for lead shot No. 7½–9. It is not a rule: coaches and experienced shooters have their own preferences.

Judging distance is hard for a beginner. Look at where you are likely to shoot the target, not where it comes from. Ask your coach or an experienced shooter in your squad: on a shooting ground that is an ordinary question.

The type of target matters too. A mini is small, so it needs a denser pattern. A battue is a thin, flat target that often flies edge-on, so you see only its thin side. It is easier to break when it turns and shows its flat face. A rabbit rolls along the ground and is tougher than a standard target.

In an over-and-under the more open choke usually goes in the barrel that fires first, and the tighter one in the second. A 1/4 and 1/2 pair (IC and M) is a popular all-round choice for many Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ stands and for a whole Compak® Sporting round, where chokes may not be changed.

Advice for beginners: do not overdo tight chokes. On the close and medium targets that beginners shoot most, a more open choke forgives small pointing errors and builds confidence. Once your technique is more consistent, you can experiment.

key_points.html: Choose the choke for the distance at which you will shoot.
A rough guide: up to 20 m cylinder or 1/8, 20–30 m IC or LM, 30–35 m M, beyond 35 m IM.
More open choke for the first shot, tighter for the second.
An IC and M pair is a popular all-round choice.
Beginners usually do better with more open chokes on close and medium targets.

did_you_know.html: Many experienced Sporting™ shooters use fairly open chokes even for far targets. They rely on precise pointing rather than on a tight pattern.

quiz.q: Which choke roughly suits a target at about 30–35 m?
quiz.explain: At 30–35 m modified is the usual choice, but this is only a guide.

quiz.q: Which barrel of an over-and-under usually gets the more open choke?

options.text: The same one in both barrels
The rules do not allow it

quiz.explain: The first shot is usually the closer one, so the first barrel gets the more open choke.

quiz.q: Why are beginners advised not to overdo tight chokes?

options.text: Tight chokes are banned for beginners
A narrow pattern forgives fewer errors
They make the recoil much harder
They wear out the barrel faster

quiz.explain: A narrow pattern needs precise pointing; on close and medium targets a more open choke forgives more.
